cards.a: Marking writes a QoS value into the packet/frame so downstream devices can treat it consistently. Markers exist at Layer 2 (802.1p CoS), Layer 3 (IP precedence, DSCP), and MPLS (EXP). Marking is trusted across the network so the core reads DSCP without re-classifying.

cards.q: What layers and bit sizes do the marking fields 802.1p CoS, IP precedence, DSCP, and MPLS EXP use?
cards.a: 802.1p CoS is L2 (3 bits), IP precedence is L3 (3 bits), DSCP is L3 (6 bits), and MPLS EXP is 3 bits. DSCP (6 bits) is the modern standard; CoS is LAN-only.

cards.q: How do IP precedence and DSCP compare in bits, classes, and default?
cards.a: IP precedence uses 3 bits (8 classes, default CS0, legacy); DSCP uses 6 bits (64 classes, default BE, preferred/modern). DSCP includes the precedence as CSx (class selector).

cards.q: What DSCP value and name are used for voice, and what is its numeric value?
cards.a: EF (Expedited Forwarding), numeric value 46, is used for voice.

cards.q: What DSCP class is used for video conferencing, and what numbers map to AF41, AF31, and AF21?
cards.a: AF4x is used for video conferencing. AF41 = 34, AF31 = 26, and AF21 = 18. AF4x = video conf, AF3x = video stream, AF2x = OAM/signaling.

cards.q: What DSCP classes are used for control traffic and best effort?
cards.a: CS6/CS7 (48/56) are used for control/routing, and CS0 (0) is best effort.

cards.q: What commands write a QoS mark into a packet, and what does each do?
cards.a: set dscp (writes DSCP), set precedence (writes IP precedence), and set cos (writes CoS). They are configured inside a policy-map class.

cards.q: How do edge and core devices treat marking, and what is needed when crossing L2/L3?
cards.a: The edge sets/re-marks, while the core trusts (does not re-mark) and queues by DSCP. CoS and DSCP need mapping tables when crossing L2/L3 boundaries.

cards.q: What is the classification/marking pairing model across the network?
cards.a: Classify then mark at the edge; the core does trust plus queue by DSCP.

cards.q: Marking is not being applied to traffic; what is the likely cause and what should you check?
cards.a: The policy is not attached to the interface (no service-policy). Check the policy-map is attached and that the set statement is correct.

cards.q: CoS markings appear lost on traffic; what is the likely cause?
cards.a: CoS is lost at an L2/L3 boundary; you need a CoS-to-DSCP mapping table when crossing between LAN and routed traffic.

cards.q: What is the difference between marking and classification?
cards.a: Marking writes a value into the packet; classification reads/identifies traffic.

cards.q: Where should DSCP be set, and what should the core do?
cards.a: Set DSCP at the edge; the core trusts the marking and does not re-mark.
